author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This code uses a recursive depth-first search to count distinct subsequences. It explores all positions in string `s` by either matching the current character with string `t` (if they're equal) or skipping it. The base case returns when we've either exhausted `s` or completed matching all of `t`, incrementing a counter for each successful match. Without memoization, it recalculates the same subproblems many times, leading to exponential time complexity and the **TLE** status.

author: Vitor + Leetcode
notes: I believe this was loosely inspired on another solution.
aiExplanation: This improves the brute force approach by adding memoization with a 2D array. The DFS explores the same states (position in `s`, position in `t`) but now stores results in `dp[i][j]` to avoid redundant calculations. When characters match, it counts both taking the character (moving both pointers) and skipping it (moving only in `s`). The recursive base cases return 1 when `t` is fully matched and 0 when `s` is exhausted without matching `t`.

author: Vitor
notes: Was expecting a TLE, somehow it passed.
aiExplanation: This replaces the 2D array with a `Map` for memoization, using a string key (`cur:lookup`) to cache results. The logic remains the same—it counts subsequences by deciding whether to skip the current character in `s` or (if it matches) include it. This approach performs well because it only stores actually-visited states rather than allocating space for the entire grid upfront.

author: Leetcode
notes: Crazy 1-dimension dp solution, seems like magic to me.
aiExplanation: This is the most optimized solution, using a 1D array instead of recursion. `dp[j]` represents the count of ways to match the first `j` characters of `t`. For each character in `s`, it iterates backwards through `t` to update the counts—if characters match, it adds the previous count (`dp[j]`) to the next position (`dp[j+1]`). This **O(n·m)** time and **O(m)** space solution is elegant and fast.
